content: 1. A systematic review and meta-analysis conducted by AE Bustinduy et al. in 2018 examined the cognitive deficits and educational losses in children infected with schistosomes. The study, published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases, highlighted the significant impact of schistosomiasis on child development and learning outcomes. 2. A 2017 systematic review and network meta-analysis published in The Lancet Global Health evaluated the effectiveness of mass deworming programs in improving the developmental health and well-being of children in lowand middle-income countries. The findings emphasized the potential benefits of such interventions in reducing the burden of parasitic infections. 3. Davis SM et al. (2015) investigated the morbidity associated with schistosomiasis in young children before and after treatment on Rusinga Island, Kenya. Published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, the study demonstrated the significant health improvements following treatment with praziquantel. 4. Stothard JR et al. (2011) explored the early detection of Schistosoma mansoni infections in young children by identifying the presence of schistosome antigens in urine, eggs in stool, and antibodies to eggs. This study, published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases, provided insights into the diagnostic timeline for schistosomiasis in pediatric populations. 5. A 2017 study by Coulibaly JT et al., published in The Lancet Global Health, assessed the efficacy and safety of praziquantel in preschooland school-aged children infected with Schistosoma mansoni. The randomized controlled trial demonstrated the drug's effectiveness and tolerability in these age groups. 6. Zwang J and Olliaro P conducted a meta-analysis in 2017, published in Parasites & Vectors, to evaluate the efficacy and safety of praziquantel at a dose of 40 mg/kg in preschooland school-aged children. The study confirmed the drug's effectiveness and safety profile in treating schistosomiasis. 7. Lo NC et al. (2016) assessed the cost-effectiveness of global guidelines for preventive chemotherapy against schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminthiasis. Published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, the study utilized modeling to evaluate the economic and health impacts of these interventions. 8. Toor J et al. (2018) analyzed the progress toward achieving the 2020 goals for schistosomiasis morbidity control using current World Health Organization guidelines. Published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, the study highlighted the challenges and successes in meeting these targets. 9. Li EY et al. (2019) examined the impact of different mass drug administration strategies on controlling Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma haematobium infections in Africa. Published in The Lancet Global Health, the study provided evidence for optimizing treatment strategies to sustain control efforts. 10. A systematic review by Burnim M et al. (2017), published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases, compared community-based, school-based, and combined delivery modes for mass drug administration programs targeting school-aged children. The findings emphasized the importance of tailored approaches to maximize coverage and effectiveness. 11. King CH et al. (2020) evaluated the impact of various mass drug administration strategies on controlling Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma haematobium infections in Africa. Published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, the study highlighted the importance of sustained efforts to achieve long-term control. 12. Olsen A et al. (2018) conducted a cluster-randomized controlled trial in Tanzania to compare the impact of different mass drug administration strategies on Schistosoma mansoni infections. The study, published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, provided evidence for optimizing treatment approaches in endemic regions. 13. Phillips AE et al. (2017) assessed the benefits of five years of different treatment approaches for urogenital schistosomiasis in Northern Mozambique. Published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases, the study was part of the SCORE project and highlighted the long-term impact of various intervention strategies. 14. Leslie J et al. (2011) evaluated the cost-effectiveness of school-based and community-distributed mass drug administration for schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminth control in Niger. The study, published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases, emphasized the economic and health benefits of these interventions. 15. Knopp S et al. (2019) conducted a cluster-randomized trial to evaluate integrated interventions layered on mass drug administration for urogenital schistosomiasis elimination. Published in The Lancet Global Health, the study demonstrated the potential for combining interventions to achieve elimination goals. 16. Obonyo CO et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on biannual praziquantel treatment for schistosomiasis. The findings, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, highlighted the effectiveness of more frequent treatment schedules in reducing infection prevalence. 17. Phillips AE et al. (2020) evaluated the impact of biannual school-based and community-wide treatment on urogenital schistosomiasis in Niger. Published in Parasites & Vectors, the study demonstrated the benefits of intensified treatment strategies in endemic areas. 18. Moussa A et al. (2016) assessed the effectiveness of semestrial mass administration of praziquantel in high-transmission areas of the Senegal River basin. Published in the International Journal of Tropical Disease and Health, the study highlighted the importance of frequent treatment in high-risk regions. 19. Sukwa TY (1993) conducted a community-based randomized trial of praziquantel to control schistosomiasis morbidity in school children in Zambia. The study, published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, provided evidence for the drug's effectiveness in reducing disease burden. 20. Gurarie D et al. (2015) modeled the long-term impact of mass drug administration on controlling Schistosoma haematobium infections in Africa. Published in Parasites & Vectors, the study provided predictions for the sustainability of control efforts. 21. Kittur N et al. (2017) defined persistent hotspots as areas that fail to meaningfully decrease schistosomiasis prevalence after multiple years of mass drug administration with praziquantel. Published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, the study emphasized the need for targeted interventions in these regions. 22. Wiegand RE et al. (2017) identified a persistent hotspot of Schistosoma mansoni infection in a five-year randomized trial of praziquantel preventive chemotherapy strategies. Published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases, the study highlighted the challenges of achieving sustained control in certain areas. 23. A multicenter randomized controlled trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of single-dose praziquantel at 40 mg/kg versus 60 mg/kg for treating intestinal schistosomiasis in the Philippines, Mauritania, Tanzania, and Brazil. Published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases, the study provided evidence for optimizing dosing strategies. 24. Osakunor DNM et al. (2018) conducted a longitudinal study on the dynamics of pediatric urogenital schistosome infection, morbidity, and treatment among preschool children in Zimbabwe. Published in BMJ Global Health, the study highlighted the importance of early intervention in this vulnerable population. 25. Danso-Appiah A et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the safety of praziquantel in individuals with or without schistosomiasis in endemic communities. The findings, published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases, confirmed the drug's safety profile across various populations.
